newsitem.title: PERU: Ikeda faults lack of information on Peru rebels.
newsitem.headline: Ikeda faults lack of information on Peru rebels.

text.p: Better information from Peru on guerrilla movements could have prevented the takeover at the Japanese ambassador's home, where rebels held 72 hostages for 126 days, Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said on Saturday.
"Regarding the movements of the MRTA (Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement), if we had had information, the crisis could never have happened," Ikeda said.
"Generally speaking, the Peruvian government, as the host nation, has the primary responsibility to ensure safety and protect (against terrorism) under the Vienna Treaty," Ikeda said.
It was the first hint of an official rebuke from Tokyo for the takeover at the diplomatic mansion in Lima, where 14 jungle-trained MRTA guerrillas stormed a diplomatic party.

Speaking to reporters here on the last day of his three-day visit, Ikeda voiced Japan's gratitude to Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori for what he called a "near-perfect" operation to end the hostage siege at the ambassador's residence.
Ikeda said he was putting the blame squarely on the MRTA for the siege, not the Peruvian government.
"More than anything else, the MRTA was entirely to blame," Ikeda said.

He said Tokyo had no way of predicting that the Japanese ambassador's home would become a target of terrorist attacks. The heavily-armed Marxist rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's home on Dec. 17 where hundreds of people gathered for a cocktail party in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito.
The rebels initially took some 500 people hostage and then gradually released most of them except for 72 prized captives.
He said terrorist movements in Peru had "drastically" subsided since Fujimori took office in 1990, opening loopholes in security measures.
Ikeda said Japan had already boosted precautionary security steps to protect its diplomatic missions around the world since the outbreak of the hostage drama in Peru.
"We have started to improve facilities and increased the number of security staff at our diplomatic missions," he said.
Asked whether Japan's assessment of Fujimori's decision to use force to end the crisis could have been different if Japanese hostages had been killed in the rescue operation, Ikeda said:
"All human lives are equally precious, so our assessment of Peru's operation would never change regardless of the identity or nationality of those who died," he said.
In Tuesday's rescue operation, all 24 Japanese hostages were freed.
"President Fujimori made a very difficult decision ... The operation was not perfect but near perfect," Ikeda said in reference to the death of three Peruvians.
Along with all 14 MRTA rebels, one Peruvian hostage and two soldiers died in the operation.
